course.learn: Cryptographic attacks target weaknesses in algorithms, protocols, implementations, key handling, or negotiation rather than trying to “break encryption” in only one way. Examples include downgrade, collision, birthday, side-channel, and weak-key attacks.
course.why: Cryptography can fail through implementation and protocol choices even when the underlying mathematics is strong.
course.example: An attacker forces a connection to negotiate an obsolete cipher suite and then exploits a known weakness in that older mode.
course.exam: Identify the attack by what is being manipulated: weaker protocol = downgrade; same hash = collision; probability-based collision search = birthday; leaked implementation behavior = side channel.

course.learn: A brute-force attack systematically tries many possible credentials, keys, or values until one works. It trades time and computing power for certainty.
course.why: Weak or short secrets make exhaustive guessing practical.
course.example: An attacker tries every four-digit PIN from 0000 through 9999.
course.exam: Brute force = exhaustive guessing. Password spraying uses a small number of common passwords across many accounts; dictionary attacks use likely words/passwords.

course.learn: A cryptographic downgrade attack forces two parties to use an older or weaker protocol, cipher, or security mode than they would normally select.
course.why: Attackers target compatibility fallbacks because old options may have known weaknesses.
course.example: A man-in-the-middle interferes with negotiation so a client falls back from a strong TLS configuration to a weaker supported mode.
course.exam: If the attacker makes security weaker by forcing legacy crypto/protocols, think downgrade.

breakdown.explanation: A birthday attack exploits the mathematics of hash collisions: finding any two inputs with the same n-bit hash generally takes about 2^(n/2) work rather than 2^n.
A hash collision occurs when two different inputs produce the same hash output. Secure cryptographic hashes are designed to make practical collisions extremely difficult.

course.learn: A birthday attack exploits the mathematics of hash collisions: finding any two inputs with the same n-bit hash generally takes about 2^(n/2) work rather than 2^n.
course.why: It explains why collision resistance requires larger hash outputs than a simple preimage-strength estimate might suggest.
course.example: An attacker searches for two different documents that produce the same weak hash so a signature on one can be abused for the other.
course.exam: Birthday = collision probability, not password birthdays or dates.

slides.title: Collision
slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.

course.learn: A hash collision occurs when two different inputs produce the same hash output. Secure cryptographic hashes are designed to make practical collisions extremely difficult.
course.why: Collisions can undermine integrity checks and digital-signature schemes that rely on a hash.
course.example: Two different files are deliberately crafted to have the same weak hash value.
course.exam: Collision resistance is a hash property. Do not confuse it with encryption-key reuse.

breakdown.explanation: Security indicators are observable signs that may reveal compromise, misuse, or abnormal conditions. Examples include account lockouts, concurrent sessions, impossible travel, blocked content, missing logs, unusual resource consumption, and resources becoming inaccessible.
